posts.topic: Mary Anning, fossil hunter of Lyme Regis
posts.image_prompt: A young woman in an early nineteenth-century bonnet, plain dress and shawl kneeling on a rocky English beach below grey cliffs, carefully chipping a large fossil skeleton of a marine reptile from the rock with a small hammer, overcast seaside light, cinematic
posts.caption:
🦴 THE WOMAN SCIENCE TRIED TO FORGET

Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, on England's south coast. Her family was poor, and they sold fossils from the crumbling cliffs to get by.

Around 1811, when Mary was about 12, her brother Joseph found a strange skull. Mary went on to uncover the rest of the skeleton — an ichthyosaur, a giant marine reptile.

In 1823 she found the first complete Plesiosaurus skeleton. Some experts at first suspected it was a fake. In 1828 she found the first pterosaur remains discovered outside Germany.

Male scientists often bought her finds and published papers without crediting her. The Geological Society, which did not admit women, didn't invite her to the meeting about her own plesiosaur.

She died in 1847, aged 47. Today the Natural History Museum calls her an 'unsung hero'.

Who else deserves credit that history gave to someone else?

posts.title: The ghost ship with no one aboard

scenes.image_prompt: A nineteenth-century two-masted sailing ship drifting alone on a grey Atlantic ocean, sails partly torn, no people on deck, fog
scenes.narration: In eighteen seventy-two, sailors found a drifting ship. Everyone aboard had vanished.

scenes.image_prompt: Sailors on the deck of a sailing ship in 1870s clothing peering through a telescope at a distant vessel, choppy grey sea
scenes.narration: It was December. The crew of the Dei Gratia spotted the Mary Celeste about four hundred miles east of the Azores.

scenes.image_prompt: Interior of an empty nineteenth-century ship cabin, wooden barrels in the hold, a captain's desk with a logbook and oil lamp, dim light
scenes.narration: The ship was seaworthy. There was about six months of food and water aboard, and its cargo of seventeen hundred barrels of alcohol was largely intact.

scenes.image_prompt: Empty davits and ropes hanging over the side of an old wooden sailing ship where a lifeboat should be, ocean below
scenes.narration: But its only lifeboat was gone. So were all ten people: Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife, their two-year-old daughter, and seven crew.

scenes.image_prompt: A Victorian writer at a desk by gaslight writing with a quill pen, stacks of magazines nearby, cozy study
scenes.narration: Theories piled up. Mutiny. Pirates. A young Arthur Conan Doyle even wrote a fictional tale about it. One modern idea: a faulty pump made the captain think the ship was sinking.

scenes.image_prompt: A tiny lifeboat on a vast dark ocean under a stormy sky, the distant silhouette of a sailing ship
scenes.narration: No one was ever found. What do you think happened? Tell us in the comments, and follow for more.

posts.caption:
⛵ Food, water, cargo — all still aboard. Ten people gone.

In December 1872, the Mary Celeste was found drifting east of the Azores with its only lifeboat missing. No one aboard was ever seen again.

Panic, mutiny or something else? Make your case 👇

posts.topic: Myth: medieval people thought the Earth was flat
posts.image_prompt: A medieval monk scholar in a candlelit stone library holding a large wooden globe of the Earth, illuminated manuscripts open on the desk without readable writing, warm golden light, cinematic
posts.caption:
🌍 DID MEDIEVAL PEOPLE THINK THE EARTH WAS FLAT?

No — and that's one of the most popular myths about the Middle Ages.

Educated medieval Europeans generally knew the Earth was a sphere. Around 1,300 years ago, the English monk Bede described the Earth as an orb, and used its round shape to explain why daylight changes with the seasons.

So where did the myth come from? Historians point to the 1800s. Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Christopher Columbus mixed fact and fiction, picturing Columbus battling scholars who feared he'd sail off the edge.

The real objections to Columbus were about distance. Critics thought the ocean crossing to Asia was far too long — and they were right. Columbus had underestimated the size of the Earth.

What 'fact' did you learn at school that turned out to be a myth?

posts.topic: Myth: sailors drank Nelson's brandy cask
posts.title: Was Admiral Nelson shipped home in brandy?
posts.hook_text: MYTH vs FACT: PICKLED IN BRANDY?

scenes.image_prompt: A wooden 18th-century naval flagship with tattered sails in heavy gunsmoke at sea, autumn light, 1805
scenes.narration: Britain's greatest admiral went home in a barrel of brandy.
scenes.label: TRAFALGAR

scenes.image_prompt: Two lines of wooden warships firing broadsides on a grey Atlantic sea, smoke clouds, distant Spanish coastline
scenes.narration: On October 21, 1805, Admiral Horatio Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar. But he was shot during the fight and died that afternoon.

scenes.image_prompt: A ship's surgeon in a Georgian naval coat standing thoughtfully below deck by lantern light, medical chest open
scenes.narration: His surgeon, William Beatty, had a problem. The voyage home would take weeks, and Nelson deserved a state funeral.

scenes.image_prompt: A large wooden cask strapped down below deck of a sailing warship, a marine guard standing beside it, lantern glow
scenes.narration: So the body was placed in a large cask filled with brandy. The spirit was drained and refilled along the way.

scenes.image_prompt: Sailors in striped shirts whispering in a dark ship's hold, one holding a tin cup, conspiratorial mood
scenes.narration: Then came the legend. Sailors supposedly sneaked drinks from the cask, calling it tapping the admiral. Rum even got the nickname Nelson's blood.

scenes.image_prompt: A grand cathedral crypt with a black marble tomb lit by candles, Georgian mourners in black
scenes.narration: The fact? There is no reliable evidence anyone drank from it. Historians treat it as a sailors' tall tale. Nelson was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.
scenes.label: MYTH vs FACT
scenes.image_search: Nelson tomb St Paul's Cathedral crypt

scenes.image_prompt: An antique wooden barrel on a moonlit ship's deck, empty tin cup beside it, calm sea
scenes.narration: Do you believe the legend? Tell us below. Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
⚓ MYTH vs FACT — ON THIS DAY in 1805, Admiral Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar and was killed in the fighting.

To bring his body home for a state funeral, it was preserved in a cask of brandy, refilled during the long voyage. That much is true.

The famous story that thirsty sailors secretly drank from it — "tapping the admiral" — has no reliable evidence behind it. Historians treat it as a sailors' legend.

Why do you think this tale has survived for more than 200 years? 👇

posts.topic: Myth: Edison invented the light bulb
posts.caption:
💡 ON THIS DAY in 1879, Edison's lab lit a bulb that glowed for over 14 hours. But Edison didn't invent the light bulb.

On October 21, 1879, at Menlo Park, New Jersey, Edison's team tested a lamp with a filament of carbonised cotton thread. It kept glowing for around 14 hours. (Records differ slightly on the exact day and hours.)

But electric light was already decades old. In 1802, Humphry Davy made a thin strip of platinum glow with electric current. In 1835, James Bowman Lindsay showed a constant electric light in Dundee, Scotland.

In England, Joseph Swan had been experimenting since 1850 and developed a working carbon-filament lamp at about the same time as Edison. Edison even bought the patent rights of two Canadians, Henry Woodward and Mathew Evans.

What Edison's team really did was make the bulb practical. Their later bamboo filaments lasted up to 1,200 hours.

The rivalry ended neatly: Edison's English company merged with Swan's to form "Ediswan".

Who deserves the credit — the first to make it glow, or the one who made it last?

posts.title: Under 40 Seconds: The Hindenburg Disaster and the Mystery of the Spark

scenes.narration: On the evening of May 6, 1937, the largest aircraft ever built hovered over a field in New Jersey. Seconds later, it was on fire. Ninety-seven people were on board.
scenes.label: 6 MAY 1937

scenes.narration: From the first sign of trouble until the bow hit the ground took only about 32 to 37 seconds. Cameras caught all of it.
In this film: why a ship designed for helium flew on hydrogen, what happened in those final minutes, and why, nearly ninety years later, the spark is still debated.
Built and launched at Friedrichshafen in Germany, the airship LZ 129 Hindenburg first flew on March 4, 1936. It was about 804 feet long, the largest rigid airship ever built.
scenes.label: 804 FEET

scenes.narration: That is almost as long as the Titanic. Yet the Hindenburg flew, because its huge body was filled with lighter-than-air gas.
It was a flying luxury hotel. One-way tickets cost 400 dollars. It had 25 double cabins, later expanded so it could carry 72 passengers, with a dining room and even a smoking room.
That smoking room was pressurised, with an airlock door to keep out stray gas. Passengers shared a single electric lighter.
The Hindenburg was designed to use helium, which does not burn. But the United States held the world's main supply, and restricted its export to Nazi Germany.
scenes.label: HELIUM

scenes.narration: So the builders filled it with hydrogen instead. Hydrogen gives even more lift than helium, but it is highly flammable, and the crew knew it.
In 1936 it made ten trips to the United States without incident. To many people, the danger seemed to be under control.
On May 3, 1937, the Hindenburg left Frankfurt for America with 36 passengers and 61 crew. Ninety-seven people in all. It was the airship's second scheduled ocean crossing of the year.
scenes.label: 3 MAY 1937

scenes.narration: Strong headwinds slowed the crossing. The ship missed its planned 6 a.m. arrival and reached Lakehurst Naval Air Station at about 4:15 that afternoon, before the landing crew was ready.
scenes.label: LAKEHURST
image_search: Naval Air Station Lakehurst Hangar No. 1

scenes.narration: Captain Max Pruss waited for a passing storm to clear before he tried to land. Just after seven in the evening, he brought the giant in.
The landing ropes dropped to the ground crew. The ship was about 260 feet up when the first flames appeared near the tail.
scenes.label: 260 FEET

scenes.narration: The hydrogen went up in a wall of flame. Within seconds the fire raced through the hull, and the burning frame sank towards the ground as people leapt clear.
Radio reporter Herbert Morrison was recording a report for later broadcast. His cry, oh, the humanity, became one of the most famous lines in broadcasting history.
Thirty-five people on board died, along with one man of the ground crew. Astonishingly, 62 people survived, some walking away almost unhurt.
scenes.label: 62 SURVIVED

scenes.narration: Among the victims was Captain Ernst Lehmann, the airline's director of flight operations, who died of his burns the next day.
American and German investigators could agree on only a few things: the fire began at the rear of the ship, and the hydrogen burned fiercely.
The leading explanation is that leaking hydrogen was ignited by a static spark, built up as the ship flew through stormy air.
Others blame the flammable coating on the ship's outer skin, or a snapping cable. Some even suggested sabotage, but no evidence for a bomb was ever found.

Whatever the cause, the film and sound recordings were seen and heard around the world, and a silent newsreel of the fire still survives. The disaster ended the era of rigid airships carrying passengers.
If the Hindenburg had been filled with helium, as its designers intended, would we all be flying in airships today? Tell us what you think. Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🔥 It was the largest aircraft ever built — and it burned in about 35 seconds.

On May 6, 1937, the airship Hindenburg caught fire while landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey, with 97 people aboard. Cameras were rolling. A reporter was recording.

This documentary tells the whole story: the floating luxury hotel with its own smoking room, why a ship designed for helium flew on hydrogen, the final approach, the astonishing number who survived — and the spark investigators still argue about.

If it had used helium, would airships still rule the skies?
